title: Alone in a Crowded Church
subtitle: A five-session study on loneliness, belonging, and the community Christ actually promised.
summary:
This study is for anyone who has stood in a full sanctuary, sung every word, shaken every hand at the door, and driven home knowing that not one person in that building could have told you what was wrong. It is for small groups, adult classes, and the church leaders who built the program and cannot understand why the people inside it are still so alone. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book Alone in a Crowded Church, on the difference between attendance and belonging, on the koinonia the first believers actually practiced in Acts, on the friendship the modern church has quietly let die, on the hospitality and the burden-bearing the New Testament commands of us toward one another, and on the long, unglamorous work of being known. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than a program.

This is not a study that scolds lonely people for not trying harder to plug in. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. The hard truth this study refuses to soften is that the church itself often manufactures the very loneliness it laments. We built buildings you can hide in. We mistook a crowd for a body and attendance for love. We made the coffee hour a performance where everyone reports that they are fine. Bell does not stand outside this indictment. He has pastored a church of hundreds and felt unknown inside his own congregation. He has asked how are you and not waited for the answer. He has let a member drift out the back door and told himself they were busy. He writes from inside the loneliness, as one of the people who helped build the room where it grows. So will you.
audience: Anyone who has felt alone in church, small groups, and church leaders

sessions.title: Alone in the Crowd
sessions.aim: To name the loneliness honestly, neither as the lonely person's failure to try nor as a problem that better programming would fix, and to admit that a full church can be one of the loneliest rooms a person ever enters.
sessions.summary: A man told Bell after twelve years of faithful attendance that if he stopped coming, it might be three weeks before anyone noticed, and he was not bitter when he said it, only tired. He was not doing anything wrong. He had done everything the church asked, joined and served and shown up, and he was still a stranger in a building full of familiar faces. The first question is not how to get people to plug in. It is why a person can be surrounded and still unknown. Bell takes the strong form of two answers that want to silence each other. The first says the lonely are responsible, that they keep to themselves, refuse the small groups, leave before the coffee, and reap the isolation they sow, and it is right that some loneliness is a wall a person builds and refuses to lower. The second says the church has done nothing wrong, that it offers groups and events and ministries, and the lonely simply will not use them, and it is right that means of connection exist and go unused. Bell will not let either win cleanly. The loneliness is not only the lonely person's fault, which refutes the first, because we built a place a person can disappear inside. And it is not solved by one more program, which refutes the second, because you cannot schedule your way into being known. It is sometimes a wall the lonely build, sometimes a room the church designed, often both. And the church begins not by adding an event but by telling the truth about the crowd it mistook for a body.

keyScripture.why: Before sin enters the world, before anything is called bad, God looks at the one man and says it is not good for him to be alone, naming aloneness as the first thing in a perfect creation that was not yet right, and treating human isolation as a problem older than the fall.

discussion.q: Before tonight, when you felt alone at church, who did you privately blame, yourself for not trying, or the church for not seeing you?
discussion.behind: Surface the default before defining anything. Most people in the room carry an unspoken verdict on their own loneliness, and it usually points inward as shame or outward as resentment. The point is not to settle it yet but to expose the assumption. Land it on honesty, not consensus, and go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: God says it is not good for the man to be alone before anything has gone wrong in the world. Why does it matter that loneliness is named as a problem in a perfect creation, not a result of the fall?
discussion.behind: Move the room off the idea that needing people is a weakness to be outgrown. Aloneness was the first not-good in a world God called good. The aim is to let people feel that the ache to be known is built into them by God, not a flaw to repent of, so they stop apologizing for needing community.

discussion.q: Bell says a full church can be the loneliest room a person enters, and that the crowd itself can hide us. Where have you felt most alone in the most crowded place?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the whole study. Do not let it become a complaint session about your particular church. Keep it on the personal recognition that proximity is not the same as being known, that a crowd can be a place to hide. The honesty here protects everyone who comes after.

discussion.q: Bell grants that some loneliness is a wall the lonely person builds and will not lower, leaving before the coffee, declining the invitation. Where might that be partly true of you?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness from the start. Not all loneliness is done to us. Some of it we guard, because being known is frightening and a wall feels safer. Make sure the room does not leave thinking they bear no part. The error is not naming the wall. It is pretending the wall is the whole story.

discussion.q: Bell confesses he has pastored hundreds and still felt unknown, and has asked how are you without waiting for the answer. Where have you done the asking that does not want a real answer?
discussion.behind: Move from diagnosis to self-implication. You are not hunting for confession to shame anyone. You want each person, the leader first, inside the indictment, because we are all both the lonely and the ones who keep others lonely. Go first.

objections.objection: If people are lonely at church, that is on them. We have small groups, we have ministries, we have a coffee hour and a sign-up sheet. The lonely ones just will not put themselves out there. You cannot make someone be known if they refuse to show up.
objections.response: Sit with the half that is true, because Bell grants it. Means of connection do exist, and some people decline every one of them and then grieve the isolation they chose, and there is a wall some build that no program can lower for them. Then make the distinction with care. A sign-up sheet is not the same as being known, and a roomful of activities can still be a place to hide in plain sight. The man who said it would be three weeks before anyone noticed had joined and served and shown up. He used the means, and was still a stranger. To answer his loneliness with one more event is to hand a thirsty man a brochure about water. The church did not fail to schedule enough. It failed to see him, and seeing is not a program.

objections.objection: Loneliness is not the church's job to fix. People are responsible for their own friendships and their own emotional lives. The church exists to preach the gospel and administer the sacraments, not to be everyone's social worker.
objections.response: Grant what is right, because there is something to it. The church is not a therapy clinic, and it cannot be reduced to meeting felt needs, and a person who treats the church as merely a friendship service has misunderstood it. Then press the other edge. The New Testament does not treat belonging as optional or extra. It commands us, dozens of times, to do things to one another, to bear, to welcome, to confess, to weep with, to carry. The community is not the by-product of the gospel. It is part of what the gospel makes. To preach the message of reconciliation while presiding over a congregation of strangers is to deny with the building what we proclaim from the pulpit.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the thing about your life right now that no one at your church knows, the thing you keep behind the answer fine when they ask how you are?
sessions.practice: This week, ask one person at your church how they are, and then do the one thing almost no one does. Wait. Do not fill the silence, do not move on after the first answer, ask a second question, and stay long enough that they could tell you the truth if they wanted to. Write down what happened, including whether you were the one who got uncomfortable first.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you said before anything had gone wrong that it was not good for the man to be alone, and we have built a church a person can vanish inside. We have mistaken the crowd for a body and the handshake for love. Forgive us for asking how are you without waiting, for letting people drift out the back, for hiding behind the word fine when we were the ones who needed to be seen. Teach us to want to be known and to do the harder work of knowing. You who set the lonely in families, do it again here. Amen.
reflection: Where have I treated my own loneliness as a weakness to hide rather than a need God himself named as not good?
What wall have I built around myself at church, and what am I afraid would happen if I let one person past it?
When was the last time I asked someone how they were and actually waited, ready to hear an answer that was not fine?
sessions.teaching: Start where Bell starts, with a man after a service. Twelve years he had come, faithfully, every week, and he told Bell, without bitterness, that if he simply stopped showing up it would probably be three weeks before anyone noticed he was gone. He was not angry. He was tired. And he was not doing anything wrong. He had done everything the church ever asked of him. He had joined. He had served. He had shown up in the rain. And he was still, after twelve years, a stranger among familiar faces. So we begin not with the question everyone wants to begin with, which is how do we get people to plug in, but with the harder and more honest one. Why can a person be surrounded by hundreds and still be utterly unknown. Until we answer that, every solution we reach for will land on the wrong wound. Take the two answers that want to silence each other, and take them at their strongest. The first says the loneliness is the lonely person's own fault. They keep to themselves. They decline the small group. They slip out before the coffee hour. They will not put themselves out there, and they reap the isolation they sowed. And this answer is not entirely wrong. Some loneliness really is a wall a person builds and refuses to lower, because being known is frightening and a wall feels safer than the risk of being seen and found wanting. The second answer says the church has done nothing wrong at all. Look at the bulletin. There are groups, classes, ministries, events, a sign-up sheet for everything. The means of connection are everywhere, and if people will not use them, that is hardly the church's failure. And this answer is not wrong either. The means do exist, and they do go unused, and you cannot force a person into fellowship they keep declining. Now watch what happens when you refuse to let either answer take the whole field. The loneliness is not only the lonely person's fault, which destroys the first position, because we built the room. We constructed buildings and services and programs in which a human being can come and go for a decade and never once be required to be known by anyone. We made it possible to belong to a crowd and to no one. But the loneliness is also not solved by one more program, which destroys the second position, because you cannot schedule your way into being known. A sign-up sheet produces attendance. It does not produce love. You can add an event to every empty square on the calendar and still send people home strangers. So here is the verdict, and the leader must hold it cleanly all the way through. The loneliness in our churches is sometimes a wall the lonely person guards, sometimes a room the church carefully designed, and very often both at once, tangled so tightly that no one can fully say where the fault begins. Some of you in this room have built a wall, and need to risk lowering one stone of it. Some of you have been failed by a community that never tried to see you, and need to hear that the failure was real and was not yours. And I have to stand inside this, in both directions, because I have been both the unknown and the one who kept others unknown. I have pastored a church of hundreds and driven home from my own building feeling like a stranger in it. And I have stood at the door and asked a hundred people how they were and not once stopped long enough to want the real answer. The how are you that does not wait is its own small cruelty, and I have practiced it for years. So before we reach for a single solution, notice where God puts this. Before sin enters the world, before anything in creation is called bad, God looks at the one man in a perfect garden and says the first not-good in the Bible. It is not good for the man to be alone. The ache to be known is not a symptom of the fall. It was built into us by God, before the fall, in a world he otherwise called good. Which means your loneliness is not a flaw in you to be repented of. It is the image of a relational God in you, telling the truth about what you were made for. That is where we begin, and it is mercy, and it is where we will go next.

scriptureStudy.note: It is not good that the man should be alone. God names aloneness as the first not-good thing in a creation he keeps calling good, before any sin, so the need to be known is woven into us by design and is not a defect to apologize for.

God settles the solitary in a home, he leads out the prisoners to prosperity. The God of Scripture takes the isolated and places them in family, which means a church that leaves people alone is working against the very heart of God.

Look to the right and see, there is none who takes notice of me, no refuge remains to me, no one cares for my soul. The psalmist names the precise ache of being surrounded and uncared for, and Scripture gives the lonely words for it rather than shaming them out of it.

Two are better than one, for if they fall, one will lift up his fellow, but woe to him who is alone when he falls. The Preacher names the practical danger of isolation, the one who falls with no one to lift him, the exact peril of the unknown member.

The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you. Paul forbids the very independence the lonely church quietly assumes, insisting that no member is dispensable and no member can opt out of being needed and needing.

By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. Jesus stakes the credibility of the whole church not on its preaching or its size but on whether its members actually love one another, which a crowd of strangers cannot.

He took with him Peter and James and John, and said, remain here and watch with me. On the worst night of his life, the Son of God did not want to be alone, and asked his friends to stay near, which tells you the need for company is no weakness.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the history the church would rather forget, because the loneliness in our buildings has a shape that did not appear from nowhere. For most of human history a person was born into a web of relationships they did not choose and could not easily leave, a village, an extended family, a parish, a guild, and the church inherited and assumed that web. The thinkers who study modern life, from sociologists of community to writers on the loss of social capital, have traced how the last two centuries dissolved that web in the name of mobility and freedom, until the modern person stands more independent and more alone than any generation before. Set this beside what happened inside the church as it adapted to that culture. We grew larger, more professional, more programmed, and in many places we quietly traded the small and demanding fellowship of people who could not avoid one another for the comfortable anonymity of a congregation a person can attend without being known. There was a real gain in it, the freedom to come without obligation, but the cost was the very thing the New Testament assumes, a body whose members are not strangers. A serious group should weigh both, the genuine good of a church anyone can walk into and the genuine loss of a church no one is required to belong to, and should ask the uncomfortable question Bell keeps returning to, whether the modern epidemic of loneliness that doctors now name a public health crisis has walked straight through the church doors and made itself at home in the very place that was supposed to be its cure. The discipline this study requires is to stop blaming the lonely and start examining the room.
sessions.caseStudy: Consider a woman in her fifties, a member of the same congregation for nine years, who teaches a children's class, brings a dish to every potluck, and stands near the doors greeting people every Sunday. By every visible measure she belongs. Then her husband leaves, quietly, and for four months she keeps coming, keeps teaching, keeps greeting, and tells no one, because she has never once been in a room at that church where the truth would have been welcome rather than awkward. When she finally breaks down in a hallway, the response is warm and immediate, a flood of people who say they had no idea and wish they had known. They are not lying. They did not know. But notice what the warmth cannot undo, that she carried it alone for four months inside a building she attended three times a week, because the church had given her a hundred roles and not one relationship in which she could have said I am not okay. Use this with the group not to assign blame but to test the study's central claim. Was her isolation a wall she built, a refusal to reach out, or a room the church designed, a place full of tasks and empty of the kind of knowing that would have caught her in the first week. The honest answer is some of both, and the discomfort of not being able to cleanly separate them is exactly where this study means to leave the room.

memoryVerse.text: Then the Lord God said, it is not good that the man should be alone.

sessions.title: What the First Church Actually Did
sessions.aim: To take seriously what the believers in Acts actually shared, to recover the word koinonia as a common life and not a coffee hour, and to refuse both the nostalgia that idolizes the early church and the cynicism that dismisses it as impossible.
sessions.summary: We talk about fellowship as though we know what it means, and we have shrunk it to a half hour of weak coffee and weather talk in a tiled hall. The first question is what the believers in Acts actually did when Luke says they devoted themselves to the fellowship, because the word he uses, koinonia, means something far heavier than sociability. It means a shared common life, a holding of things in common, a partnership so real it reached their houses and their money and their bread. Bell takes the strong form of two objections. The first is nostalgia, the longing to copy Acts exactly, sell everything, hold all things in common, and treat the early church as a blueprint we have betrayed, and it is right that we have lost something they had. The second is cynicism, that the Acts community was a brief, miraculous, impossible moment that fell apart almost immediately and cannot be reproduced, and it is right that it was not a permanent utopia. Bell will not let either win. We cannot simply copy their economics, which checks the nostalgia, because the text describes what love did, not a law it laid down. But we cannot dismiss it as impossible either, which checks the cynicism, because what made them a community was not a program but a devotion, and devotion is available to us. They were together. They were in homes. They were known down to their needs. The turn is that koinonia is not an event the church holds. It is a life the church shares, and we have settled for the event because the life costs more.

keyScripture.why: They devoted themselves to the apostles teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers, listing koinonia alongside doctrine and the table and prayer as one of the four things the first church gave itself to, not an optional extra but a central devotion of the new community.

discussion.q: When someone says fellowship at church, what picture comes to your mind, and how far is that picture from a shared common life?
discussion.behind: Open by exposing the shrunken word before the exegesis. Most will picture coffee and small talk, and that gap is exactly what Bell wants to examine. The aim is to feel how small we have made a word that once meant holding life in common, so the rest of the session can fill it back up.

discussion.q: Luke lists the fellowship right alongside the apostles teaching, the breaking of bread, and the prayers. Why does it matter that being known by one another sits next to sound doctrine as a core devotion, not an extra?
discussion.behind: Move the room off treating community as the soft, optional part of church life. Luke ranks it with teaching and prayer. The aim is to let people see that a church can be doctrinally sound and still disobedient if its members are strangers, because the fellowship is commanded, not suggested.

discussion.q: The first believers were in one another's homes, sharing meals and needs. Why do you think so much of their common life happened around tables in houses rather than in a public hall?
discussion.behind: Press on the location of belonging. Real knowing tends to happen at a table in a home, not in a lobby. The aim is to surface the practical truth that the church grew close where it ate together in small spaces, and to make the room wonder where that has gone in their own life.

discussion.q: Bell takes the cynic's view that the Acts community was a brief, impossible moment we cannot copy. What is true in that, and what does it miss about what actually made them a community?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The cynic is right that we cannot legislate their economics or pretend it was permanent. The miss is that what bound them was a devotion, not a program, and devotion is open to anyone. Help the room separate the copyable heart from the unrepeatable details.

discussion.q: Bell admits his own church has a fellowship hall and almost no fellowship, a building for the thing it does not actually do. Where have you settled for the event because the shared life costs more?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. Many of us attend the gathering and avoid the actual knowing, because the gathering is safe and the knowing is costly. Go first, name where you have chosen the easy version. The point is honest recognition, not a plan to fix it tonight.

objections.objection: The Acts church sold everything and held all things in common. If we were serious, we would do the same, and anything less is a betrayal of the real church. We should copy them exactly.
objections.response: Bell honors the longing under this, because something real has been lost and the nostalgia is grief for it. Then he refuses the literalism. Luke is describing what love spontaneously did, not laying down a law the church must replicate, and even in Acts the sharing was voluntary, not commanded, since Peter tells Ananias the property and the proceeds were his to do with as he chose. The point was never the economics as a rule. The point was a love so real it reached people's possessions. To turn that into a mandatory blueprint is to copy the outward form and miss the heart, which was that no one among them was in need because they actually saw one another. Reproduce the seeing. The generosity will follow from it, as it did for them, rather than the other way around.

objections.objection: That was a unique, Spirit-filled, honeymoon moment in the very first days of the church, and it fell apart almost immediately, with complaints and divisions within a few chapters. You cannot reproduce it. It is naive to try.
objections.response: Grant the realism, because it is partly right. The Acts community was not a permanent utopia, the cracks show up quickly, and anyone who promises to recreate a flawless early church is selling a fantasy. Then mark what the cynic misses. What made them a community in the first place was not a momentary feeling or a one-time miracle. Luke says they devoted themselves, a word of sustained, deliberate commitment, to teaching and table and prayer and one another. Devotion is not a honeymoon. It is a discipline, and it is available to any church willing to pay for it. The early church was not magic. It was committed. We have plenty of feeling and very little devotion, and that, not some lost miracle, is the actual gap between us and them.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If your real needs, the financial one, the marriage one, the fear you carry alone, were actually known by your church the way the first believers knew one another, which need would you most want them to see, and which would you most dread them seeing?
sessions.practice: This week, do the most ordinary and most lost thing the first church did. Share a meal in a home, yours or someone else's, with at least one person from your church, with no agenda but to be together and to ask real questions. No event, no program, just a table. Write down what was said at that table that would never have been said in a church lobby.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, the first believers gave themselves to one another the way they gave themselves to your word and to prayer, and we have kept the word and the prayer and quietly let the one another go. We built a hall for fellowship and forgot what the word means. Forgive us for trading a shared life for a half hour of small talk because the real thing costs more than we wanted to pay. Teach us to devote ourselves, not to feel a feeling but to commit a life, to open our homes and our tables and our actual needs to one another. Make us a body again, and not a crowd. Amen.
reflection: What have I shrunk the word fellowship down to, and what would it mean to let it grow back to the size Luke gave it?
Where in my life is there a table, a home, a small enough space, in which I could actually be known, and have I been avoiding it?
What would change in my church if being known by one another were treated as seriously as sound teaching and faithful prayer?
sessions.teaching: We use the word fellowship constantly, and we have almost no idea what it once meant, because we have shrunk it down to a half hour of weak coffee and talk about the weather in a tiled hall we actually named the fellowship hall, as though the building could do the thing the people will not. So the question for this session is simple and unsettling. What did the first believers actually do when Luke says they devoted themselves to the fellowship, because whatever it was, it was not what happens between our services. The word Luke uses is koinonia, and it does not mean sociability. It means a common life, a holding of things in common, a partnership so deep and so real that it reached into people's houses and their meals and their money. Luke spells it out. They were together. They had all things in common. They were selling their possessions and distributing to anyone who had need. They broke bread in their homes, day by day, and ate with glad and generous hearts. This is not a coffee hour. This is people whose lives had become genuinely intertwined, who knew one another down to the level of need and met it, who ate together so often and so openly that no one among them went hungry or unseen. Now take the two objections at full strength, because both are honest. The first is nostalgia. It reads Acts and aches, and it concludes that the only faithful response is to copy them exactly, sell everything, hold all things in common, and treat any church that does not as a betrayal of the real thing. And there is truth here. We have lost something they had, and the longing is grief, and the grief is right. But the literalism misreads the text. Luke is describing what love did, freely, spontaneously, not a law the apostles imposed, and Scripture itself makes this plain when Peter tells Ananias that his property and his money were his own to keep or to give. The sharing was voluntary. It flowed from a love that had first learned to see. To turn it into a mandatory economic blueprint is to grab the outward form and drop the heart, which was never the common purse but the common life that made the purse natural. The second objection is cynicism. It says this was a brief, Spirit-drunk honeymoon in the first weeks of the church, that it fell apart almost immediately, complaints about the daily distribution by chapter six, division not long after, and that it is naive to think we could ever reproduce it. And there is truth here too. The Acts church was not a flawless utopia, the cracks appear fast, and anyone promising to recreate a perfect early church is selling you something. But watch what the cynic misses, because it is the whole point. What made them a community was not a feeling and not a one-time miracle. Luke says they devoted themselves. That is a word of sustained, costly, deliberate commitment, the same devotion they gave to the apostles teaching and to the breaking of bread and to the prayers. Notice that list, because it is the verdict of this session. Koinonia stands right next to sound doctrine and the Lord's table and prayer as one of the four pillars the first church gave itself to. Not an extra. Not the soft part. A core devotion, ranked with teaching and prayer. Which means a church can have flawless doctrine and faithful prayer and still be disobedient, still be failing, if its members remain strangers to one another, because being known together is not the garnish on the gospel. It is part of what the gospel makes. And here I have to confess the gap in my own house, because my church has a fellowship hall and almost no fellowship. We built a room and named it for a thing we do not actually do in it. We have the gathering. We have lost the shared life, and I have let us lose it, because the gathering is cheap and the life is expensive. It costs an open home, an open calendar, an open admission of need, a willingness to be seen at the table where you cannot keep performing fine. Devotion is not a honeymoon feeling we lost. It is a discipline we have refused to pay for. So the recovery does not begin with copying their economics or manufacturing their emotion. It begins where they began, in homes, around tables, in small enough spaces that a person cannot stay hidden, with people who decide that being known by one another is as non-negotiable as being taught and praying. They were together. They were seen. No one among them was in need, because no one among them was unknown. We have settled for the event because the life costs more. That is the gap, and it is the only gap, and it is one we could close if we were willing.

scriptureStudy.note: They devoted themselves to the apostles teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers. The fellowship is listed beside teaching and prayer as a core devotion, which means a church of strangers is not merely less warm but is actually disobeying one of the four things the first church gave itself to.

All who believed were together and had all things in common, selling their possessions and distributing to all, as any had need. Their common life reached all the way to their money, which is the proof that they actually knew one another down to the level of need.

Day by day, breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts. The center of their fellowship was the table in the house, not the public assembly, which tells you where being known is most likely to happen.
The full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul. Luke describes a unity so deep it touches heart and soul, a oneness no program produces, the fruit of a love that had learned to see.

There was not a needy person among them, for distribution was made to each as any had need. The result of real knowing is that need does not go unmet, the exact opposite of a church where a person can quietly struggle for years unseen.

A complaint arose because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. Even the first church had cracks and overlooked people, which guards us against an impossible nostalgia and proves that community is maintained by attention, not magic.

If we walk in the light, we have fellowship with one another. John ties koinonia to walking in the light, to honesty rather than performance, which means fellowship grows where people stop hiding and not where they stay polished.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the rich layers of the word koinonia, because the New Testament uses it for far more than friendly gathering and recovering its range exposes how thin our version has become. The word carries the sense of partnership, of a share held jointly, of participation in something common. Paul uses it for the believers shared participation in the body and blood of Christ at the table, for the partnership of churches in the work of the gospel, even for the sharing of money he gathers for the poor in Jerusalem and calls a koinonia. So fellowship in Scripture is not first a feeling of warmth among people who like one another. It is a shared participation in Christ that necessarily binds his people to one another, vertical and horizontal at once, communion with God producing communion among the communed. Set this beside the modern Western instinct, shaped by centuries of rising individualism, to treat faith as a private transaction between the soul and God with the church as an optional support service, and you can see why our fellowship has thinned to coffee. We have kept the vertical and amputated the horizontal, as though a person could share in Christ without sharing in his body. A serious group should weigh the older voices who refused that split, who insisted that there is no such thing as a solitary Christian, that the New Testament has no category for the believer who belongs to Jesus but not to a people, and should ask honestly whether our private faith and our public loneliness are two symptoms of the same disease. The discipline here is to recover koinonia as a participation that has hands and a table, not a sentiment that has a name tag.
sessions.caseStudy: Consider a young couple, new to the city and new to the church, who attend faithfully for half a year and then stop, and no one can quite say why. They came to the services, smiled at the right moments, signed up for a newcomers event that was pleasant and forgettable, and were invited, once, to a small group that met in a fellowship hall and consisted of an hour of structured discussion followed by everyone going home. What they were starving for, without the words to name it, was a table in a home, a meal that ran long, a relationship that did not end when the program did. They never got one, not because anyone was unkind, but because the church's entire apparatus of connection happened in the building and on the calendar, and the building closes and the calendar empties. Compare this to a second couple in the same church who were, in their first month, simply invited to dinner at an older member's house, with no agenda, and then invited again, and who six years later are deeply rooted. The difference was not a better program. It was a table in a home. Use this with the group to press the session's claim, that koinonia is a shared life and not an event, and to ask honestly where in their own church the life actually happens, in the public hall or in private homes, and what it would cost them to open a table of their own.
