glossary.definition: The ache of being unknown, of having no one who could tell what is actually wrong in your life or would notice if you disappeared. The study treats it not as a single thing but as sometimes a wall the lonely build and sometimes a room the church designed, often both, and refuses to flatten it into only one.

The New Testament word usually translated fellowship, meaning a shared common life, a partnership, a holding of things in common, and a participation together in Christ. In Acts it reached into homes and meals and money, far heavier than the coffee hour we have shrunk it down to.

Being known and held within a body, as distinct from merely attending it. The study argues belonging is not finally manufactured by effort but received in Christ, who has already made us one body and members of one another before we earn a place.

Presence in the room, being counted and participating, which a person can do for decades without ever being known. The study names the distance between attendance and belonging as the central problem it exists to address.

The dozens of New Testament instructions addressed to one another, to love, bear, welcome, confess, weep with, encourage, and serve, which together form the practical job description of the church and which it most consistently ignores.

The biblical command to open your own actual home and table to others, especially those who would otherwise be alone, not the hosting of a church event in a public hall. The study treats it as one of the two precise antidotes to loneliness.

The deliberate carrying of a weight that is not yours for the sake of another, which Paul says fulfills the law of Christ, making a church where everyone carries alone a place that is breaking that law rather than merely lacking warmth.

Bonhoeffer's name for the idealized picture of community we carry in our heads, which destroys real fellowship by demanding from actual flawed people a perfection they can never deliver. The cure is to receive the people God has actually given.

Paul's image for the church as a single living organism whose members are joined to one another, so that if one suffers all suffer, the opposite of a congregation where a person can suffer for years unnoticed. The status we already hold in Christ.

The deep, loyal, costly friendship Scripture honors in Jonathan and David and in Ruth and Naomi, a bond that refuses to leave and will tell the truth, distinct from the disposable acquaintance the modern church too often settles for.

The habitual practice, especially common in church, of answering the question how are you with the word fine when it is not true, the small daily refusal to be known that keeps the lonely lonely even in a warm room.

The modern public health crisis of isolation, in which chronic loneliness damages the body as severely as heavy smoking and more people than ever report having no one to confide in, a secular confirmation of the not-good God named in the garden.

The deepest human longing, named by Paul, to be seen all the way down and not abandoned, fulfilled first in God who already knows us completely and loves us anyway, which becomes the security from which we can risk being known by people.

promoKit.inviteCaption: You can be surrounded by hundreds of people at church and still be completely unknown. A five-session study on loneliness, belonging, and the community Christ actually promised, drawn from Alone in a Crowded Church. It is honest that the church often builds the loneliness it laments, and it never tells you to just try harder. Come honest, not finished.
quoteCards: You can attend a church for forty years without ever once belonging to it. Attendance is presence. Belonging is being known.
It is not good for the man to be alone. That was the first not-good thing in a perfect world, before any sin. Your loneliness is not a flaw. It is the image of a relational God in you.
We built a fellowship hall and forgot what the word means. We kept the gathering and quietly let the shared life go, because the real thing costs more.
Jesus did not call his disciples his students or his staff. On the last night of his life, he called them his friends. Friendship is not beneath the dignity of the church.
Bear one another's burdens, Paul says, and so fulfill the law of Christ. A church where everyone carries alone is not merely cold. It is breaking the law of Christ.
The risk of being known is the possibility of being hurt. The refusal to be known is the certainty of being alone. And aloneness is the worse wound.
You do not have to build the body. He built it on a cross. You only have to stop standing in it as a stranger.
We made the coffee hour a place where everyone is required to report that they are fine. Then we wondered why no one knew anyone.
